title: 4. Industry Structure, Competitive Moat & External Learning Hub

epigraph.quote: “Mostly, we lose only if it is a cost parameter which comes in.”
epigraph.author: Vijay Gupta, Founder, Chairman and CEO, SoftTech Engineers, Q4 FY2026 earnings call, 2 June 2026

web_blocks.html: Start by naming the market, because a moat only means something inside a defined castle. SoftTech supplies three different products to overlapping customers. The first is statutory permit software: a municipality's rule engine and workflow that reads an architect's CAD or BIM drawing, checks it against the city's building bye-laws (called development control regulations, or DCR) and routes the file to officers for sanction. The second is works and infrastructure monitoring for government departments, airports and ports. The third is private-sector construction software plus new transaction platforms such as Mumbai's digital exchange for transferable development rights (TDR, a tradable certificate given to landowners whose land the city acquires). The permit business is the core. Management said CivitPERMIT was 50% of FY2026 revenue and CivitINFRA 25% [16]. The company's February 2024 deck put AutoDCR, the permit product's earlier name, at ₹40.7 crore of ₹65.3 crore standalone FY2023 revenue, or 62% [18].

Now the number everyone repeats: roughly 80% share of Indian permit automation. It appears in the September 2018 investor deck (“~80% Market Share” and “Largest market share in India (80%) for building plan approval management system”) [17], in the 2021 AGM deck (“80%+ Authorities in India use CIVIT Permit”) [19] and in the February 2024 deck (“over 80% of market share in India in its domain”) [18]. None of them says who measured it, what the denominator is, or as of what date.

The company's own papers pull that number in different directions. The 2018 deck counted 3,700+ urban local bodies and called 80% of them “still untapped”, while 340+ were live [17]. The 2021 deck counted 600+ agencies [19]. The FY2026 annual report says 1,500+ cities against “substantially more than 4,000” statutory urban local bodies, so at most about 37% by head-count, and it does not repeat the 80% claim [15]. When an analyst put “80% market share in permitting” to the CEO on the 2 June 2026 call, he answered about TDR and neither confirmed nor corrected it; the only share he volunteered was “29-30%” for STRUDS, the structural-design product transferred to a UK company in 2011 [16]. My reading: 80% described the installed base of drawing-reading scrutiny engines among authorities that had already chosen automation by 2018. It is not a measured share of today's market, and I would not carry it forward.

web_blocks.takeaway: The credible rivals are local and public: a state IT department's chosen vendor, a free government platform, and Indian firms writing the same kind of rule engine. The global names are mostly partners or adjacent.

web_blocks.html: Read the table with one filter: who actually wins tenders against SoftTech? The global names in the usual list (Autodesk, Bentley, Nemetschek, Trimble, Oracle Primavera) are mostly partners or adjacent. The annual report treats Autodesk, Dassault, Bentley and Esri as complements, and RuleBuddy is built on Autodesk's AutoCAD OEM engine [15]. Trimble matters only historically, because it now owns the structural business SoftTech divested in 2011 [16]. I found no source showing any of them contesting an Indian municipal permit tender, and no evidence that Oracle Primavera overlaps any SoftTech product, so I have left it out rather than invent a rivalry.

The sharpest evidence of a real rival is Telangana. The state introduced TG-bPASS in September 2020, and the legacy portal still reads “Designed & Developed by : SoftTech Engineers Limited” (TG-bPASS portal). In December 2024 it launched BuildNow to replace it, promising scrutiny of a three-tower, 40-storey project in under two minutes [22]. The BuildNow portal credits Deepwork Technologies Private Limited as developer. SoftTech's February 2024 deck still listed a Telangana state order among its reference wins [18]. A statutory system that lasted about four years is not the permanent lock-in that the word moat implies.

In fairness, SoftTech won state business in the same period: a ₹33 crore, five-year Andhra Pradesh order (APDPMS 2.0) disclosed in its Q1 FY2026 presentation, and a further Gujarat mandate for CivitPERMIT [15]. One more data point is ambiguous. Uttar Pradesh's building-approval portal, labelled “Developed on AutoDCR Platform”, carries a notice that all application submissions were suspended from 20 June 2026 (UPOBPAS). The page does not say why, so I treat it as an open question to ask management, not as a loss.

web_blocks.caption: Moat evidence and missing evidence
headers: What would strengthen or weaken it
rows: Codified local rules

Weakens as states unify rulebooks and AI codifies rules faster; strengthens if new states adopt the rule engine
Embedded workflow (switching cost)
Officers, architects and fee collection run through the system; migration needs retraining [15]
Telangana replaced its system in about four years [22]; the next state to leave would show the pattern
Government qualification
CMMI level 5 and reference deployments help meet tender eligibility [15]
Eligibility gets you bidding; the award goes to price (see below)
Pay-per-use annuity
₹31.72 crore in FY2026, up 38.6%, charged to applicants per square foot [15][16]
Q2 FY2027 SaaS revenue grew only 11.9% [21]; depends on permit volumes and on states letting a vendor charge citizens
Data and AI
CEO calls permit data “a gold mine” [16]; twelve-agent CivitTWIN launched [15]
The annual report concedes better general AI “reduce[s] the value of holding” a dataset [15]
Platform breadth
Seven Civit platforms; JNPA port twin order of ₹92.95 crore [21]
Outside permits the lines are small: CivitBUILD 2.8% and eTDR 3.2% of H1 FY2027 revenue [21]
web_blocks.takeaway: The moat is real in how hard it is to rip out a working permit system, but it has been breached once and its second leg, the rule codification, is eroding.

web_blocks.html: The company's argument for stickiness is fair. Once a municipality's officers, architects and fee collections run through one system, replacing it means data migration, retraining and a period of double handling, and the annual report says so [15]. The localisation work is also real, because each city's bye-laws must be turned into machine-checkable rules. But two forces are shrinking that second advantage. States are consolidating rulebooks: Maharashtra's UDCPR, notified in December 2020, applies to all planning authorities except Greater Mumbai and a few others (The Hitavada), which means fewer rule sets to codify and a smaller head start for whoever codified the old ones. And the annual report itself concedes the AI risk: new entrants do not have the dataset, but “improvements in general-purpose reasoning reduce the value of holding one” [15]. Telangana's replacement was marketed on scrutiny speed and “advanced technologies” [22], which is exactly that threat.

Pricing power is where management was most candid. In a government tender, L1 means the lowest bidder and L2 the second lowest. On Oman, the CEO said: “From the pricing front, we are at L2 in the tender... But from the technology front, we were T1,” and the customer wanted a lower price after a Singapore bidder came in lower [16]. Asked about lost bids, he said: “it could be about 70% winning and 30%, sometimes losing because of cost or something. Mostly, we lose only if it is a cost parameter which comes in” [16]. Read plainly, product quality gets SoftTech onto the shortlist, price decides the award, and the company does not claim a premium. Its pricing power appears after the award, in per-permit fees and maintenance contracts.

The second structural weakness is the payer. The annual report calls government procurement and payment cycles the company's “most material commercial exposure” and quantifies it: days sales outstanding (the average days between billing and cash) of 260 [15]. The CFO explained one slice: “in government businesses, the government uphold some 1%, 2% of our invoice values, which they will process after certain period of time,” and the CEO added that retentions can take “sometimes even seven years” to come back [16]. This is not new. The May 2018 prospectus already reported that 37.22% of trade receivables were more than six months past due and that state and central government supplied 70.86% of revenue. Eight years later the problem is smaller, not solved.

Concentration compounds it. FY2026 was the first of the three years I checked (FY2024 to FY2026) in which a customer crossed 10% of revenue: two customers together contributed ₹26.1 crore, 19.7% of consolidated revenue [15][20]. The report counts 18 states, the same number as the February 2024 deck's “18+” [15][18]. My reading is that growth has come more from deeper wallet share inside known governments (Gujarat, the Airports Authority, the Mumbai TDR platform, the port authority) than from new states. That is less costly to win, but it ties results to a few counterparties and their payment calendars.

web_blocks.region_era: United States, 1998–2024; software for local, state and federal government
web_blocks.mechanism: Tyler entered the software business in 1998 and has not paid a dividend since [24]. It supplies a broad set of mission-critical applications (permitting and civic services, ERP, property tax, courts, public safety) to government agencies and keeps them on maintenance or subscription contracts that renew automatically unless the client gives notice; after acquiring NIC Inc. in April 2021 it also supplies payment services into the same client base [24]. The moat is breadth across many departments of the same customer plus recurring revenue.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Calendar 2024: revenues $2,137.8 million; subscriptions 62.8% and maintenance 21.7% of revenue (recurring about 84%, $1.8 billion); subscription revenue up from $350.6 million in 2020 to $1.3 billion in 2024, including $698.2 million of transaction-based fees; GAAP operating income 14.0% of revenue; accounts receivable $587.6 million, about 100 days of revenue (my arithmetic) [24].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Government software compounds when the vendor owns many workflows of one customer and moves from one-off licences to renewing subscriptions and per-transaction fees. SoftTech's pay-per-use model is the same instinct at small scale: usage-linked revenue is about 24-25% of its sales against Tyler's 84% recurring base, and Tyler is roughly 140 times SoftTech's revenue at ₹88 per dollar (my assumption). Even Tyler's receivables run near 100 days; SoftTech's 260-day DSO says it has not yet earned that quality.

web_blocks.region_era: India, FY2011–FY2017; technology and content supplied to government and private schools
web_blocks.mechanism: Educomp's EduReach business set up and ran IT labs in government schools on a build-own-operate-transfer model: it spent first and was paid quarterly by state governments over three to five years [25]. Management described the revenues as “predictable & locked in for three to five years” [25]. The risk is the one SoftTech names in its own annual report: governments pay when they pay, while the vendor carries the upfront investment and, here, the borrowing that funds it.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: FY2012 consolidated (₹ million): income 14,912.8 versus 13,509.0 (+10.4%); trade receivables 8,650 versus 5,070 (+70.6%), equal to 58% of income or about 212 days (my arithmetic); net profit 1,355.4 versus 3,366.7 (−59.7%); finance charges 1,432.5 versus 1,089.9; cash and bank balances 838.4 versus 2,097.5 [25]. The company has been under insolvency resolution since 30 May 2017 [26].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: A contract that is “locked in” guarantees work, not cash. For SoftTech the watch-list is receivables-plus-unbilled work growing faster than sales, the expected credit loss provision, and borrowing. The cushion is real: gross borrowings plus lease liabilities were about ₹39 crore against equity of about ₹170 crore at March 2026 [15], far from Educomp's leverage. The shared mechanism is slow public payment funding growth.

web_blocks.html: Put the two side by side and the lesson is about structure, not size. Tyler's moat is breadth across many departments of the same customer, and even there receivables run near 100 days of revenue [24]. Educomp's trouble started with receivables growing roughly seven times faster than sales, for customers that were governments [25][26]. SoftTech's pay-per-use model is the right instinct, because fees collected from applicants bypass the slow treasury cycle, but it is a quarter of revenue, not four-fifths. The leverage cushion is the difference from Educomp; the breadth and the recurring base are the gap from Tyler.

My judgement: SoftTech has a real but narrower moat than the 80% story implies. It is strongest where a state has embedded the product into its statutory workflow and lets the company charge applicants per permit. It is weakest where a state can rewrite the rules or procure something new on speed or price. The evidence supports a durable niche vendor with good products and ordinary pricing power, not a monopoly. The next test is whether a second Telangana happens.

External Learning Hub — Watch the SoftTech corporate video (YouTube, “30 Years of Transforming the AECO Industry”), then try the product demo page and read the CivitPERMIT and CivitTDRx pages to see what an officer or applicant actually uses. For the rivals, open the Telangana BuildNow portal, the UPYOG building plan approval module, CSM Technologies' BPAS page and CSII's explainer on Auto-DCR. For the global view, see Solibri (rule-based BIM checking) inside the Nemetschek brand list and Tyler Technologies' 2024 annual report. Primary documents: the FY2026 annual report and the 2 June 2026 earnings-call transcript.

Picture a municipal engineer in a mid-sized city on the day the new permit software goes live. Until then her desk was a stack of rolled drawings and a ledger. Now an architect uploads a CAD file, the engine measures setbacks and floor-area ratios, and the file arrives with a list of objections already written. She likes it, because her discretion, and the arguments that come with it, have shrunk. That is why such a system is hard to remove once it runs. It is also why a state minister, watching permit timelines on a dashboard, can decide that a faster engine from someone else is worth the disruption. Both things happened in India within a few years of each other [15][22].

Here is a question to put to the CEO and the CFO together: when you say you hold about 80% of the market, which authorities are in the denominator, and who counted them? A second question follows: if the answer is that the share is by count of authorities that chose automation, what is your share of the authorities that have not? The annual report says there are more than 4,000 urban local bodies and that 1,500 are served [15]. A good manager answers precisely and does not mind being asked. A defensive answer would tell you something too.

Buffett has said that what matters in a business is the durability of its competitive advantage, not the excitement of its industry. Apply that to a permit vendor. The advantage is not the software, which a well-funded rival can rebuild. It is the fact that a statutory record, once digitised, becomes a public asset that officials do not want to migrate. Telangana shows that the asset can still be moved when a government decides it should be. The question is how often that happens, and the sample so far is one state in a base of eighteen [18][15].

In plain words, then: SoftTech is a good specialist in a market where its customers are also its regulators and its payers. Specialists in that position earn decent margins when they are on the shortlist and wait a long time for their money. Judge the moat by repeat awards, by how many states return to tender, and by how the pay-per-use share holds as permit volumes change, and not by the 80% slogan [16][21].

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A moat for a government software vendor is a statutory habit that officials are reluctant to break, not a patent. SoftTech has that habit in many cities, and its own CEO says it loses tenders on price. The Telangana switch shows the habit can be broken. Watch repeat awards, the pay-per-use share and the next state tender before trusting the 80% slogan.
